content:
A woman was escorted onto a police vehicle at dawn after her clothing was suspected of carrying seditious intent.

While officers removed the woman, several other officers repeatedly directed journalists to leave, telling them to go to the press area, and extended the orange cordon towards Ying Wa Street. Once the woman had boarded the police vehicle, they retracted the cordon.

T-shirt printed with Japanese characters

"Court-watching companion" Ah Wai, who queued near the woman, said she was wearing a black T-shirt printed only with Japanese characters, and he could not understand why police considered the shirt seditious. Ah Wai said he had been around the West Kowloon Court area on Tuesday evening, when he already saw a group queuing. Officers at the time asked him to leave via Ying Wa Street, saying, according to Ah Wai, "no queuing tonight," without giving a reason. Ah Wai said he understood but did not认同 the Hong Kong Alliance's past stance, and regarding the verdict, he said he was mentally prepared, adding, "I want to see how the judge writes the judgment."

"Court-watching companion" Ah Wai said the woman was wearing a black T-shirt with only Japanese characters on it.

Police ban Tang Yuet-kwan from bringing "Tiananmen" reports into court

Former standing committee member of the Hong Kong Alliance Tang Yuet-kwan arrived this morning with a Ming Pao report on the "Tiananmen" incident dated 11 June 1989, a report on the "30th anniversary of Tiananmen" from 2019, and a batch of bookmarks printed with "Commemorating the 22nd anniversary of June Fourth" and "100th anniversary of the Xinhai Revolution", intending to queue for a seat in the public gallery.

He was told by police that the items bore wording such as "Hong Kong Alliance" and "vindicate June Fourth," as well as Sun Yat-sen's "the revolution is not yet successful, comrades still need to strive," and could not be brought into the court. If he wished to queue, police would hold the items for him. He said he told police he would not display the items inside the court but was still refused, so he decided not to enter and would wait outside the court for the verdict.

"As I understand it, these are not yet illegal items"

Asked why he insisted, he said, "I feel that at this moment, before the verdict, I think there may be a grey area. I feel that for the time being these items ... as I understand it, they are not yet illegal items. So if they [the police] say they are suspected of being something [seditious], or feel like prohibited items, I cannot accept that. If I do not agree, why should I appear to be disarmed? To make this kind of bottomless compromise?"

Regarding the verdict, Tang said it was up to the judge and he would take it calmly, but personally did not believe the Hong Kong Alliance was guilty. He added that if the Alliance were convicted, it would overturn established legal understanding: "One country, two systems is not dead, but at the very least it is clearly a severe step backward."

"Long-haired woman" arrives to queue at night

Activist "Long-haired woman" Lei Yuen-lin went to queue overnight carrying only a plastic bag containing her ID card, a pack of tissues and a phone, to avoid having items registered or searched by police.

Sister Lin said she visited one of the defendants, Lee Cheuk-yan, last week and found him in good spirits. She said Lee had read in the newspaper about her fight for better labour rights in extremely hot weather and told her not to queue, "because he knew about the queueing party and didn't want us to suffer."

Sister Lin said she visited one of the defendants, Lee Cheuk-yan, last week and found him in good spirits.

Sister Lin, herself a sanitation worker, said she saw bins outside the court filled to overflowing this morning, describing it as "unprecedented." After an elderly cardboard collector wheeled away two carts of cardboard, the situation did not improve. During the interview, officers approached again and told Lin to leave, saying they would "have someone come and clear [the rubbish] later" and "it's no big deal."

Sister Lin, herself a sanitation worker, said she saw bins outside the court filled to overflowing this morning, calling it "unprecedented."

Suspected queueing-party members kept dumping black garbage bags into nearby bins in the morning. Once the bins had piled into a mountain of rubbish, they moved on to dumping waste on the kerb in front of Ying Wa Primary School.

Suspected queueing-party members dumped rubbish on the kerb and covered it with a tarpaulin.

Suspected queueing party dumps rubbish on kerb, hides it under tarpaulin

Reporters observing on site noted that those at the head of the queue kept dumping black garbage bags into nearby bins throughout the morning. After the bins had piled into a mountain of rubbish, they moved on to dumping waste on the kerb in front of Ying Wa Primary School and covering it with a tarpaulin. One woman wearing a straw hat and mask went straight back to the registration area to rejoin the queue after dumping the rubbish. A contractor cleaner from the Food and Environmental Hygiene Department later arrived around 7am to help the elderly cardboard collector deal with the rubbish pile. The female cleaner said, "It only happens when the court is in session. If there's no session, there's none of this!"

Main court issues 65 tickets, queueing party moves in on Tuesday

The main court only issued 65 tickets, and together with seven extension courts, a total of 553 tickets were issued.

The queueing party had already moved in outside the court on Tuesday (the 18th), queuing three days in advance. With the thunderstorm warning in force yesterday morning and heavy rain for a time in the afternoon, the queueing party's contingent laid tarpaulins on the ground. By around 4pm yesterday, some of the queueing party were sleeping on the ground, while others took out nail clippers to trim their fingernails outside the court. More than 30 people remained at the scene, and all had to register their details with officers stationed there when entering and leaving.

The queueing party moved in on Tuesday and laid tarpaulins on the ground during rain on Thursday.

On Thursday afternoon, suspected queueing-party members took an afternoon nap.

Suspected queueing-party members trimmed their fingernails outside the court.
